questions.solution: The Ghadar Party was formed in San Francisco, USA, in 1913 by Indian revolutionaries such as Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, and Kartar Singh Sarabha. Its goal was to liberate India from British rule through an armed struggle.

The British Government enacted the Champaran Agrarian Law in 1918, prompted by Mahatma Gandhi's 1917 Champaran Satyagraha Movement. This movement sought to end the coercive cultivation of indigo on farmers' lands in the Champaran district.

The Cabinet Mission arrived in India in 1946 with the purpose of discussing the modalities for the ultimate transfer of power from British rule to Indian hands. It played a crucial role in formulating proposals for the formation of a united and self-governing India, ultimately leading to the creation of the Mountbatten Plan and the subsequent partition in 1947.

The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 was the first satyagraha movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in British India and is considered a historically important rebellion in the Indian independence movement. It was India's first Civil Disobedience movement launched by Mahatma Gandhi to protest against the injustice meted out to tenant farmers in the Champaran district of Bihar.

The All-India Muslim League was formed on December 30, 1906, in Dhaka. It was a political organization that aimed to represent the interests of Indian Muslims during the period of British colonial rule.

The Home Rule League was established in 1916 by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant. It was divided into two branches - one led by Tilak in Maharashtra and Central Provinces, and another led by Annie Besant in the rest of India. The movement aimed at achieving self-government for India within the British Empire.

· The Salt Satyagraha (Dandi March), initiated by Mahatma Gandhi on March 12, 1930, was a pivotal event in India's freedom struggle.

· Gandhi and his followers marched 240 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to protest the British salt tax, symbolizing defiance against colonial oppression.

· This nonviolent campaign mobilized millions of Indians, sparking widespread civil disobedience and uniting the nation against British rule.

Key Impact:

· The Salt Satyagraha globalized India's freedom struggle and solidified Gandhi's strategy of Satyagraha (nonviolent resistance).

· Swadeshi Movement (1905 - 1911): Focused on boycotting British goods (pre-Gandhian era).

· Gadar Movement (1913s): A militant diaspora-led effort, not nonviolent.

· Quit India Movement (1942): Launched later, demanding immediate British withdrawal.

Gandhiji envisioned that by aligning the non-cooperation movement with the Khilafat Movement, which aimed to protect the interests of Muslims regarding the Caliphate, Hindus and Muslims could unite in their struggle against colonial rule. This strategy aimed to foster Hindu-Muslim unity as a potent force against British imperialism.

The Poona Pact was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar in 1932. It aimed to address the concerns of the depressed classes regarding political representation by ensuring separate electorates for them within reserved seats, as opposed to the Communal Award proposed by the British that would have granted them a fixed number of seats but without separate electorates.

· The Quit India Movement, also known as the August Movement or Bharat Chhodo Andolan, was a mass civil disobedience movement launched by Mahatma Gandhi on 8 August 1942 during World War II.

· It demanded an immediate end to British colonial rule in India.

· Gandhi gave the famous slogan "Do or Die" (Karo Ya Maro) to Indians, urging them to fight for complete independence.

The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 was Mahatma Gandhi's first major civil disobedience movement in India, where he fought against the exploitative indigo cultivation system imposed by British planters on local farmers.

· The Khilafat Movement (1919 - 1924) was a pan-Islamic political protest campaign launched by the Ali brothers (Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali) along with Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and other leaders. Its aim was to pressure the British government to preserve the Ottoman Caliphate, which many Indian Muslims regarded as a symbol of Muslim unity and leadership.

· It also became a part of the larger Indian freedom struggle, and Mahatma Gandhi supported it as a unifying movement between Hindus and Muslims.

· It eventually merged with the Non-Cooperation Movement led by Gandhi.

Wahabi Movement

· Timeframe: 1820s onwards

· Leader: Syed Ahmed Barelvi

· Objective: To revive Islamic principles and purify Islam by removing un-Islamic practices; later turned into a militant movement against British rule.

Ahmadiya Movement

· Timeframe: Late 19th century

· Founder: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad

· Objective: Reform Islamic practices, promote peace, rational thinking, and oppose religious violence.

Faraizi Movement

· Timeframe: 1830s

· Founder: Haji Shariatullah

· Objective: To reform Muslim society by focusing on religious duties (Faraiz) and removing un-Islamic customs.

· Region: Bengal

· Later Leader: Dudu Miyan, who gave it a more anti-landlord and anti-British character.

· Significance: It was both a religious reform and socio-political movement.

• Full Name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi

• Born: 2 October 1869, Porbandar, Gujarat

• Died: 30 January 1948, New Delhi

• Education: Studied law in England; later went to South Africa, where he began his political activism.

• Satyagraha: Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent resistance, first practiced in South Africa and later in India.

• Champaran Movement (1917): First successful Satyagraha in India, supporting indigo farmers in Bihar.

• Kheda Satyagraha (1918): Protested against tax collection during famine conditions.

• Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22): Urged Indians to boycott British institutions.

• Civil Disobedience Movement (1930): Launched with the Dandi March, breaking the salt law.

• Quit India Movement (1942): A mass protest demanding an end to British rule, launched with the slogan "Do or Die".

• Role in Partition: Advocated Hindu-Muslim unity and opposed the partition of India.

• Death: Assassinated by Nathuram Godse on 30 January 1948.

Lala Hardayal started the Ghadar movement in the early twentieth century among Indians in North America, primarily Sikhs, to end British rule in their country of India. On July 15, 1913, the Ghadar Party was founded in Astoria, Oregon.

He founded the Ghadar Party in the United States. This party's members were expatriates who wanted to start an international movement against British rule in India. On July 15, 1913, the Ghadar Party was founded in Astoria, Oregon.

The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922) was led by Mahatma Gandhi to resist British rule through non-violent means. However, it was called off after the Chauri-Chaura incident in February 1922, where a violent clash between protestors and police resulted in the burning of a police station and the death of 22 policemen. Gandhi, emphasizing non-violence, withdrew the movement following this event.

Hence, option (3) is the correct answer.

The Hindu Mahasabha was established in 1915 as a reaction to rising concerns about Muslim fundamentalism and political activism during that period. It aimed to advocate for Hindu interests and promote Hindu nationalism as a response to perceived threats to Hindu identity and culture.

Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as Frontier Gandhi, founded the Khudai Khidmatgars (Servants of God) movement. It was a non-violent resistance movement against British rule, primarily active in Northwest Frontier Province (now in Pakistan).

The Chauri Chaura incident occurred at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district of the United Province, (modern Uttar Pradesh) in British India on 4 February 1922, when a large group of protesters, participating in the Non-cooperation movement, clashed with police, who opened fire. In retaliation the demonstrators attacked and set fire to a police station, killing all of its occupants. The incident led to the deaths of three civilians and 23 policemen. Mahatma Gandhi, who was strictly against violence, halted the Non-cooperation Movement on the national level on 12 February 1922, as a direct result of this incident.

· The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed the British government to imprison people without trial.

· Gandhi launched the Rowlatt Satyagraha in protest.

· The Rowlatt Act (officially known as the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act) was passed in March 1919 by the Imperial Legislative Council.

· It authorized the British government to imprison people without trial, restrict civil liberties, and conduct trials without juries.

· Gandhi strongly opposed this act and launched a non-violent protest movement against it.

· This opposition eventually led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in April 1919, when British troops fired on unarmed protesters in Amritsar, killing hundreds of people.
